lead: In the last days before Lent the Church opens the first page of the Bible and, beside it, a short scene from Mark. Genesis shows God bringing order out of darkness by his word alone. Mark shows crowds running through the villages with their sick, begging only to touch the edge of a cloak. The psalm gives the response of a creature who looks at all this and says, “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” The God who said “Let there be light” has come near enough to be touched.

set: This is the opening of the whole Bible, and the Lectionary divides the account: today the first four days, tomorrow the rest. Many scholars think this page received its final form among Israel's priests around the time of the exile in Babylon, in the sixth century BC. The Babylonians had their own stories of creation, in which the world came out of a war among the gods, and they honoured the sun, moon and stars as divine. Genesis tells a different story: one God, no battle, and a world that is good.

The writer uses the picture of the world known in his day, with a dome overhead and waters above and below it. The Church does not read this page as a lesson in astronomy. It teaches, in the form of a solemn hymn, who made the world and what the world is for (Dei Verbum 11–12).
str: vv. 1–2: the beginning: earth without form, darkness, the deep.
vv. 3–5: day one: light, separated from darkness.
vv. 6–8: day two: the dome, separating the waters.
vv. 9–13: day three: dry land and seas, then plants.
vv. 14–19: day four: the lights in the dome.

¶ The days have a pattern. The first three make spaces, and the next three fill them: the lights on day four belong to the light of day one. Each day has the same refrain: God said, it was so, God saw, evening and morning.
kw: In the Old Testament this verb has only God as its subject. It never mentions any material or tool, so it suits an act that belongs to God alone.
A rhyming Hebrew phrase for what is empty and without shape. God's first work is not to destroy this chaos but to bring it into order.

One word for all three. The NRSV says “a wind from God”; the POC says God's chaitanyam, and many Christian readers have heard the Holy Spirit here. Both readings keep what matters: God's own power is moving over the waters.
Said four times in today's reading and seven times in the chapter. It means both good and beautiful, as a thing is when it fits its purpose.
vv: Then God said, “Let there be light”; and there was light.
No struggle and no effort. God speaks and it is. St John begins his Gospel with the same words, “In the beginning”, and calls this creating Word a person.
And God saw that the light was good; and God separated the light from the darkness.
God does not call the darkness good, but he gives it a limit and a name (v. 5). Nothing in the world stands outside his rule, not even the night.
God made the two great lights

Genesis does not use the usual words for sun and moon here, only “the greater light” and “the lesser light”. Many scholars think the writer chose this on purpose: to neighbouring peoples these were gods, and here they are lamps hung up to mark the seasons.
ch: The Catechism says that Scripture presents the Creator's work “symbolically as a succession of six days” (CCC 337), and draws from it that nothing exists that does not owe its existence to God, and that each creature has its own goodness (CCC 338–339). The Church confesses that creation is the common work of the Father, the Word and the Spirit (CCC 290–292). She proclaims this same page at the Easter Vigil, by the light of the paschal candle, because the Resurrection of Christ is the beginning of a new creation.

r.h: Even the fringe of his cloak
set: This is one of Mark's summary passages, in which he sums up many days in a few lines. It comes straight after Jesus walks on the water, a scene that ends with the disciples unable to understand, “for their hearts were hardened” (6:52). Gennesaret is the fertile plain on the north-western shore of the Sea of Galilee. They had set out for Bethsaida (6:45) but land here, and the crowds find them at once.
str: vv. 54–55: people recognize him and run to fetch the sick.
v. 56: villages, cities and farms; the sick laid in the marketplaces; all who touch him are healed.
kw: The edge of a garment, and perhaps the tassels that the Law told Israelites to wear on their clothes (Numbers 15:38). So Jesus is seen here as a faithful Jew in the dress of his people.
Mark's verb at the end of v. 56 is the ordinary word for “save”. The NRSV rightly says “healed”, but the Greek hints at more than bodily cure.
vv: When they got out of the boat, people at once recognized him,

The disciples in the boat have just failed to understand him, and the people on the shore know him immediately. They do not yet know the whole truth about him, but they know where to bring their pain.
and rushed about that whole region and began to bring the sick on mats to wherever they heard he was.
A whole district on the move, carrying those who cannot walk. The healing depends in part on the people who do the carrying.
and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his cloak; and all who touched it were healed.

They have probably heard of the woman who was healed by touching his cloak (5:27–29). There is no magic in the cloth. The power is his, and the touch is an act of faith that even a person with no words can make.
ch: The Catechism draws a line from this scene to the sacraments: the sick try to touch Jesus, and in the sacraments Christ continues to “touch” us in order to heal us (CCC 1504). The Word of creation has taken flesh, so God's power can now reach us through what is seen and touched: water, oil, bread, a hand laid on the head.

qa: No. Genesis teaches that the world comes from God and is good; it does not teach how many years creation took or how the sky is built. St Augustine warned Christians not to speak foolishly on natural matters in the name of Scripture (in substance). The Catechism welcomes scientific study of origins (CCC 283) and says that there can never be a real conflict between faith and reason, since the same God gives both (CCC 159). The order of the days serves the message: that is why there is light on the first day and a sun only on the fourth.
study: The people of Gennesaret carried their sick to Jesus. Whom could you bring to him this Lent, by prayer or by going with them?
What in your own day would change if you looked at the created world and said with God, “it is good”?
